At 3:17 every morning, the town’s streetlights went out.

Not flickered. Not dimmed. Went out—as if someone, somewhere, reached up and pinched the glowing wires between two fingers.

No one knew why.

The mayor blamed the power company. The power company blamed old infrastructure. The old infrastructure, if it could speak, would probably have blamed the mayor.

People adapted. They carried flashlights. They left porch lamps on. Parents taught children not to fear the dark, though they themselves watched the windows until the lights returned at 3:18.

Everyone except Mara.

Mara had been awake at 3:17 for twenty-two years.

She had been born at 3:17 in the morning during a thunderstorm that split the sky above the hospital. Her mother liked to say the whole world had gone dark to make room for her.

Her mother died when Mara was six. Her father died when she was seventeen. Her husband left at thirty-two, taking the dog and the blue ceramic bowls. At forty, Mara stopped counting the things that left.

She became the town librarian because books stayed where you put them.

Every night, at 3:16, she walked between the shelves with a ring of keys and checked the locks. The library had once been a bank, and the old vault still stood behind the history section. Inside, the town stored newspapers, census ledgers, property maps, and all the small evidence by which a place proved it had existed.

At 3:17, the lights went out.

Mara would wait in the dark for one minute.

At 3:18, they came back.

Then she would open the vault.

She had not told anyone what she was looking for. Not even herself, exactly. She only knew that after her father’s funeral, she had found a phrase written on the back of an old receipt in his desk:

*When the lights go out, look for the missing year.*

There were plenty of missing years in the town archives. Fires. Floods. Clerical errors. One entire winter lost when a pipe burst and ink ran into the basement drains.

But Mara had searched all of them.

On the twenty-second anniversary of her birth, she found a box she had never seen before.

It was small and gray, tucked behind a shelf of municipal budgets. There was no label. No date. Only a brass keyhole.

Mara tried twelve keys before the seventh one turned.

Inside lay a single photograph.

It showed the town square, though not the town as she knew it. The clock tower was taller. The courthouse was painted white. In the center of the square stood a crowd of people wearing dark coats and looking toward the camera.

At first Mara thought the photograph had been taken in winter.

Then she saw the snow was ash.

In the back row stood her father.

He looked young—perhaps twenty-five—with a cut across his cheek and one hand resting on the shoulder of a little girl.

The girl was Mara.

Not the Mara she remembered, with scraped knees and missing teeth. This girl was perhaps four years old, and she was holding something bright in her palm.

Mara brought the photograph close to the desk lamp.

A match.

On the back, in her father’s handwriting, were six words:

*We burned the old town down.*

For a long time, she heard only the hum of the lights.

Then the library clock struck 3:17.

Darkness filled the room.

Mara turned the photograph over again. Her own small face seemed to shift in the absence of light. The girl’s eyes were open, fixed on something beyond the camera.

Something behind Mara.

She did not turn around.

In the dark, a child began to breathe.

Slowly. Carefully.

Mara’s fingers closed around the photograph.

“Why?” she whispered.

A voice answered from the history shelves.

“Because it was hungry.”

The lights returned.

There was no one there.

Only a trail of ash across the floor, beginning at the vault and ending beside the children’s section.

Mara followed it.

The children’s books were arranged in bright rows: animals, fairy tales, planets, trains. At the very bottom, behind a stack of old picture books, she found a door no taller than her knee.

It had not been there yesterday.

She opened it with the brass key.

Beyond was a staircase descending into warm darkness.

Mara thought of calling the police. She thought of calling the mayor, the power company, anyone who might answer and say that this was ordinary, that doors did not appear in libraries, that dead fathers did not leave warnings in locked boxes.

Instead, she took a flashlight from the desk.

Then she went down.

The stairs ended beneath the town.

There were houses there, or the outlines of houses, built from charred beams and blackened stone. A school. A church. A bakery with its oven still glowing red. The old town, buried beneath the new one.

At the center stood a tree with silver leaves.

Hanging from its branches were hundreds of small glass bulbs. Each one held a flickering light.

Mara recognized the glow. It was the same glow as the streetlamps.

A figure stood beneath the tree.

Her father.

He had not aged.

“You took too long,” he said.

Mara’s flashlight trembled. “You’re dead.”

“Yes.”

“Why did you burn the town?”

He looked up at the silver leaves.

“Because it learned how to keep people.”

Around them, the buried houses creaked.

“People disappear here,” he continued. “Not die. Disappear. A mother walks into a room and forgets her children. A boy goes to school and never comes home, though everyone remembers seeing him. A wife wakes beside her husband and cannot remember his name. The town feeds on what we love most.”

Mara thought of her mother. Her father. The blue bowls. The dog.

“Did it take them?”

“It took what it could.”

“And me?”

Her father’s expression broke, just slightly.

“No. You were the one thing it couldn’t digest.”

The bulbs above them began to swing.

One by one, lights went dark.

Above, in the town, streetlamps vanished.

3:17.

The silver tree bent toward Mara, its roots cracking through the floor.

Her father held out a match.

“You have to finish what we started.”

Mara stared at the tiny flame.

“What happens if I do?”

“The town burns again.”

“And if I don’t?”

He looked toward the staircase.

“Then everyone wakes tomorrow with someone missing.”

Mara struck the match.

For one second, its flame was the smallest light in the world.

Then she touched it to the roots.

The tree screamed.

Aboveground, every streetlight burst at once—not into darkness, but into fire. Windows glowed. Roofs caught. The town square filled with people stumbling into the streets, calling names they had forgotten they knew.

Mara stood beneath the earth while the old town burned.

Her father reached for her hand.

This time, she let him take it.

When morning came, there was no library, no courthouse, no clock tower. Only a field of black soil and a single silver tree, its leaves turned to glass.

Mara was gone.

But at 3:17 the next morning, the streetlights stayed on.

All except one.

In the window of an empty house at the edge of town, a small lamp glowed blue.

And from inside came the sound of a child laughing.
